transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could face a House vote on impeachment later this week.
Kentucky Republican Congressman Thomas Massey filed an impeachment resolution Monday
as a House opened back up following the midterm elections.
Here's NPR's Sam Greenglass.
Massey says he doesn't know if there are enough votes to impeach,
but he really only needs a couple of Republicans, which is totally possible.
Now, if Hegseth is impeached in the House, it's up to the Senate to hold a trial,
and over there it would take 67 senators to convict, which is a very high bar.
Hegseth says he's not worried about the effort
and is planning to address it at a press conference in the morning,
his first at the Pentagon in six months.
President Trump told reporters at the White House that he will stand by Hegseth.
He also called Congressman Massey a stone-cold loser.
In Alaska's U.S. Senate race, Democrat Mary Peltola has increased her lead
over Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The Alaska Division of Elections updated its count Monday
and one of the nation's most closely watched Senate contests,
the Associated Press, has not yet called the race.
Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin reports.
Peltola now leads by 2,500 votes.
She's just over one percentage point ahead of Sullivan,
but she's still below 50 percent in the four-way race.
If that remains the case, the state will conduct an instant runoff.
The fourth-place finisher will be eliminated
and his ballots reallocated based on his voters' next choices.
In the Alaska governor's race,
Democrat Jonathan Christ Tompkins retains a substantial lead.
Tens of thousands of first-choice ballots are expected to be tallied by Friday,
and the ranked choice tabulation will be November 18.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
The Senate race in Mississippi has also yet to be called.
Election officials say Democrat Scott Colom leads
Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by some 2,500 votes.
The French government alleging that Iran's Revolutionary Guard
was behind last month's cyber attack that hacked hundreds
of supermarket refrigeration systems across the country,
costing millions in spoiled food.
Iran has yet to respond to the accusations.
Rebecca Rossman has more from Paris.
The French foreign minister called the attack "unprecedented"
and suggested Iran would face more EU sanctions.
The Paris prosecutor's office, meanwhile,
says it has opened an investigation into a cyber unit
linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
It began in October with a cyber attack on some
700 commercial fridges and freezers across France,
sending temperatures soaring to over 120 degrees Fahrenheit.
Some fridges even caught fire.
Supermarkets were forced to throw away millions of dollars
worth of spoiled food.
Last week, other countries in Europe were hit with similar attacks.
It's unclear if the incidents are linked.
Rebecca Rossman, NPR News, Paris.
This is NPR.
Voters in California have rejected a ballot measure
that would have taxed the wealth of billionaires.
The tax would have been the first of its kind in the nation,
with much of the money raised through it
going toward making up for federal funding cuts to health care.
Opponents argue the tax would have prompted
the ultra-wealthy to leave the state.
A Utah judge has set a trial date for the man accused of killing
prominent conservative activist Charlie Kirk last year.
The judge Monday set a June 2028 trial date
for 23-year-old Tyler Robinson,
who was pleaded not guilty to the seven counts against him.
Kirk was fatally shot during an appearance at Utah Valley University.
Nation's public schools are educating a million fewer students
than before the pandemic, but as NPR's Janaki Mehta reports,
school districts are not yet shutting down or cutting staff, as many expected.
All over the country, communities have been having difficult,
often emotional conversations about whether districts
should close schools to save money.
One in four public schools has enrollment
that's at least 15 percent below where it was before the pandemic.
But a new study from Stanford University
finds that the number of operating schools across the nation
and teachers employed at those schools
has actually increased since before COVID.
There are more teachers per student than at any time in the last 15 years,
yet researchers warn that tight budgets
and shrinking student populations are a reality
school leaders are going to have to address soon
if they don't want essential services
like mental health support to be compromised.
Janaki Mehta and PR News.
And I'm Giles Snyder.
This is NPR News.
Give what students need right when they need it
at donorschoose.org/local.

topics.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could face House impeachment vote after Rep. Thomas Massey's resolution
President Trump says he will stand by Hegseth and calls Massey a loser
Alaska Senate race: Democrat Mary Peltola extends lead over Republican Dan Sullivan
Alaska governor's race: Democrat Jonathan Christ Tompkins retains substantial lead
Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,500 votes
France accuses Iran's Revolutionary Guard of cyber attack on supermarket refrigeration systems
California voters reject tax on billionaires' wealth aimed at offsetting federal health care cuts
Utah judge sets June 2028 trial date for Tyler Robinson in Charlie Kirk killing
US public schools enroll a million fewer students than pre-pandemic, but school closures not yet happening
